book_context: The plot runs as a chain of small coincidences. Tommy's overheard name leads to Whittington, the advertisement brings Carter and Julius, and the survivor list yields Rita. Each lead opens the next, and Mr. Brown repeatedly strikes just ahead of them. Chapters IV–VII set up the governing premises: the Danvers/Lusitania backstory, the draft treaty, and the Brown method. That method means a nondescript, overlooked figure behind someone else, a common name, and the unanswerable 'one of us'. These chapters also introduce Julius, with his genealogy and the single photograph, and tie Rita to the name Marguerite. Later revelations depend on all of this: the identity of Mr. Brown, the false Jane at Manchester, the photograph in Julius's drawer, Annette's 'Marguerite' cry, and the 29th. Early chapters must plant these premises neutrally, without foreshadowing the solution.

essential: Keep the passage of time and the economy: forty pounds; the advertisement appeared on Thursday; letters came on Friday; Tommy promised not to open them; they meet at the National Gallery.
Keep Tommy's teasing pretence that the advertisement failed, then the reveal of two answers. Keep Tuppence's outburst and the 'clergyman's daughter' exchange, at least briefly.

Read both letters. Carter's comes from 27 Carshalton Gardens at eleven. Julius P. Hersheimmer writes from the Ritz, asking them to call about lunch-time. Tommy's joke about a 'Boche' or a millionaire and 'free food' sets up the next chapter.
Tommy's comic rehearsal of saying 'Edward Whittington!' to Carter can be compressed, but its premise must stay: it mimics Tuppence's 'How much?' scene.
Carter's entrance: tired manner, attractive smile, magnetism. He turns the question back on them ('what do _you_ know?') and Tuppence resists.
Tommy recognizes Carter from Intelligence work in France. Carter answers 'No names, please'; the house is lent by his cousin, so the work is unofficial. Tuppence tells the whole story.
Carter's offer: work for him unofficially, expenses paid, a moderate salary ('screw'), and the task 'Find Jane Finn'.

The Danvers story in causal order: the draft treaty drawn up in neutral America in 1915; Danvers carries it on the Lusitania in an oilskin packet; his body is found but the packet is missing; he was seen speaking to a young American girl; he was possibly shadowed. She is Jane Finn, an orphan pupil teacher going to a Paris hospital, traced across Ireland and then lost. The treaty went unused, so it was assumed destroyed.

Why it matters now: the treaty was once a weapon for Britain and is now a weapon against it. It implicates statesmen and could serve Labour as a party cry, but the real danger is Bolshevist gold and the unknown man behind them, 'Mr. Brown'. Keep Carter's hedges ('I do not believe in its likelihood myself', 'in my opinion').

Brown's profile: believed English, not German; aims probably at supreme power; always plays a secondary part, behind a nonentity. Tuppence recalls the clerk called Brown; no telephone in the outer office, so the 'message' was an order from someone who had overheard everything.
Carter's concern for 'such young things', and the 'look after each other' exchange.

The puzzle: the revolutionaries claim to hold the treaty yet are wrong about its provisions, and the cipher explanation won't work. They are seeking information about Jane from Carter's side. Carter's hypothesis of a false Jane in Paris, and Tuppence realizing that was the plan for her. Carter is speculating here; present it as speculation, not fact.
optional: The cheap day, the walking and the picture house (para 1) can shrink to a single clause.
Trim Tuppence gazing at the Turners and Tommy's 'favourite picture' tease to a line, but keep the joke's premise if the reveal of two answers stays.
Tuppence's preference to open the rich-looking envelope last can go.
The Carshalton Terrace description ('ladylike looking houses', the respectable maid) is removable.
Carter's aside on secret diplomacy and 'Somebody always talks!' can be cut or reduced.
The hospital staff's surprise and the passport detail can compress into 'she never arrived in Paris'.
Carter's remark on Labour government and British trade can be shortened, provided 'the _real_ danger' still leads to Brown.
The repeated 'Mr. Y. A.?' greeting can be cut if the advertisement's signature is clear.
risks: The long exposition paragraphs may tempt over-quotation; compress them in Carter's voice rather than quoting at length.

voice_profile: Light, brisk comic-thriller narration. The narrator is close to Tommy and Tuppence and mildly ironic about them, with mock-formal phrasing such as "Mr. Beresford obliged" and "Nobody did, which was the great thing." Most of the effect comes through dialogue. The two leads trade slangy banter ("old thing", "old bean", "Don't be a wretch") and deflate each other's vanity. They parody detective fiction and formal speech: plans of campaign, "Proceed, O Sherlock!", "a literary flavour". Tuppence frankly loves money; Tommy is slow, practical and deadpan. Mr. Carter speaks in a tired, reflective monotone of hedged exposition. Julius uses American idiom ("Put me wise", "Sure thing", "I guess") and gets things done by forceful, moneyed impatience. Menace arrives suddenly in a short closing line after comedy. The text uses double hyphens for breaks and interruptions, four-hyphen trailing-offs, ellipses, and underscore emphasis.

essential: Tuppence's 'meant to be' and Carter's admitted superstition about luck and fate continue the coincidence theme.
Carter's warning that the pace may be forced: the coup was planned for the new year, but government action against strikes may bring things to a head. They may have little time.
Carter's terms: funds, information, and no official help if they get into trouble with the police. Tuppence will write out a list of questions.
Tuppence's money exchange: her complaint about government blue and green forms, Carter laughing, money sent by return of post, three hundred a year each, her 'beautiful accounts'.
Outside, Tommy whispers Carter's real name; it is not given. 'He's IT!', Tuppence's steel image, the pinch, and 'We've got a job!'
They remember Hersheimmer and take a taxi (all expenses paid). Keep the blackmailer joke.
Julius: younger than expected, about thirty-five, square and pugnacious, very little accent. He states at once that Jane is his cousin and gives the exact relationship.
He doesn't know where she is and turns suspicious (the 'Sicily' line). Tommy gives a guarded account and calls them private inquiry agents.

Julius has never seen Jane. His father quarrelled with Aunt Jane over her marriage to Amos Finn. The father made his fortune and died last fall, Julius's conscience stirred, and he hired a man who found that the parents were dead and Jane a Lusitania survivor.
Julius contacted Scotland Yard and the Admiralty. A man came 'this morning' for the photograph. Julius plans to go to Paris tomorrow and offers to 'buy her off' if she is in trouble.

At lunch, Inspector Japp's card arrives. Julius explains that the photograph is the only copy, from a college principal. Tuppence feels dread, and the morning visitor's name is revealed as Inspector Brown.
optional: Tommy's chuckle about Whittington 'getting the wind up' can be cut.

Tuppence's 'When did you last see the dece--' detective-fiction slip can be cut, but if kept, keep the premise that it is borrowed from detective fiction.
The details of the father's career in oil, steel and railroads can compress.
The menu (oysters, Sole Colbert) can go.
The 'just as you might be' brother-and-sister misunderstanding can be cut.
risks: The ending must stay a cliffhanger; do not import the next chapter's confirmation that Inspector Brown was unknown to Scotland Yard.

essential: The narrator draws a veil: Inspector Brown was unknown to Scotland Yard, the photograph is lost for good, and Brown has triumphed again.
The set-back brings them close to Julius. They tell him everything; his remark on 'moss-grown' English girls; the move to the Ritz justified as keeping in touch with Jane's only relation.
Breakfast banter: Tuppence demands action, while Tommy applauds, cites his 'union' and keeps reading the Daily Mail.
Clue one: Whittington, with Tommy's thousand-to-one objection, Tuppence's coincidence law, and the flag-tray idea punctured by meals.

Clue two: 'Rita'. Tuppence reasons that Danvers was shadowed, probably by a good-looking woman, who must have survived, since otherwise the gang could not know Jane had the papers. Tuppence admits it is 'only a chance'.
Carter sent the survivor list in reply to her questions, but most entries give only Mrs. or Miss, which complicates things. She lists the London addresses.
Tommy's Voting Register ruse at The Laurels: Mrs. Edgar Keith is Eleanor Jane; the servant's 'about the gas' line; Tommy's male smugness, which Tuppence concedes.
Lunch summary of the blanks, with Sadie's suffrage lecture. Mrs. Vandemeyer is next; Tuppence is discouraged and Tommy cheers her.
The banter about Brown having not yet 'done us to death' and Tommy's 'moles in the dark'. Its irony must remain.
At South Audley Mansions: 'Margaret', corrected to 'g u e'; Tommy's bold 'Rita Vandemeyer'; confirmation that Marguerite is her name.
They rejoice. Tuppence pulls Tommy into the shadow beside the lift, two men pass, and she tells him to follow because the bigger one is Whittington.

Miss Wheeler the lady's maid can be cut.
The tour of England, Ireland and Scotland can be cut.
risks: Tuppence's woman-shadower reasoning must stay framed as her guess, not as established fact.

essential: Tommy follows the pair. His bookish ideas of shadowing meet reality (the taxi worry); they let a taxi pass and head to Oxford Street.
At Lyons' he sits behind Whittington. Boris is described as fair, weak-faced, about fifty, Russian or Pole, with shifting eyes. Whittington gives orders and addresses him as Boris.
Fragments overheard: 'Ireland', 'propaganda', no Jane Finn. The Flossie line: she 'gets the voice right'. 'only in an emergency'.

The Brown exchange: Boris says the name is common and chosen for that reason, and that Brown may be a fable of the Inner Ring. Whittington's 'You may have met him already.' Boris's 'one of us' musing.
At Waterloo, Whittington buys a first-class ticket to Bournemouth on the 3.30; Tommy buys the same. Boris's 'nearly half an hour' prompts Tommy's dilemma.
Tommy phones Julius at the Ritz ('Sure. I'll hustle'). He has only a few shillings left after the ticket. The clock ticks down to 3.29 and Julius arrives.
Julius has 'only' three or four hundred dollars; Tommy gives him the ticket and Whittington. Julius boards as the train leaves.
Tommy trails Boris by tube to Piccadilly Circus, along Shaftesbury Avenue and into Soho, to a dilapidated cul-de-sac square. Boris knocks with a peculiar rhythm.
Tommy, against his usual sober common sense, copies the knock. The villainous doorkeeper says 'Well?'; Tommy says 'Mr. Brown?' and is directed upstairs to the second door on the left.
